solution: Take O as the origin and mark the directions N, S, E, W in the usual way. Draw the ray OP making an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the northward direction ON, measured towards the east. Choosing the scale 1 unit \(= 10\) km, cut off OP of length 4 units, and put the arrowhead at P. Then \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) represents the required displacement of 40 km, \(30^\circ\) east of north. Resolving along east \((\hat{i})\) and north \((\hat{j})\), \(\overrightarrow{OP} = 40(\sin 30^\circ\,\hat{i} + \cos 30^\circ\,\hat{j}) = 20\hat{i} + 20\sqrt{3}\,\hat{j}\).
10 kg measures mass, which has magnitude only and no associated direction. Hence it is a scalar.
2 meters north-west specifies both a magnitude (2 m) and a direction (north-west). Hence it is a vector.
\(40^\circ\) is the measure of an angle, which has magnitude only and no direction associated with it. Hence it is a scalar.
40 watt measures power, which has magnitude only and no associated direction. Hence it is a scalar.
\(10^{-19}\) coulomb measures electric charge, which has magnitude only and no associated direction. Hence it is a scalar.
\(20\ \text{m/s}^{2}\) measures acceleration, which is the rate of change of velocity and therefore possesses a direction as well as a magnitude. Hence it is a vector.
Time period is measured by its magnitude alone and no direction can be assigned to it. Hence it is a scalar quantity.
Distance is the length of the path actually covered; it has magnitude only and no direction. Hence it is a scalar quantity.
A force is specified only when both its magnitude and the direction in which it acts are given. Hence it is a vector quantity.
Velocity is speed together with the direction of motion, so it has both magnitude and direction. Hence it is a vector quantity.
Work done is the scalar product of force and displacement, and the result is a number carrying no direction. Hence it is a scalar quantity.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key names the wrong pair as coinitial. Read off the figure, the two vectors that share an initial point are the top edge and the left edge, which both begin at the top-left corner. The key is refuted by its OWN remaining entries: its answer to part (ii) requires the right and left edges to both run downwards, and its answer to part (iii) requires the top and bottom edges to be opposite — both of which hold only under the reading given here. Entry (i) is the sole outlier.] Coinitial vectors are those having the same initial point. In Fig 10.6 the arrow \(\vec{a}\) along the top side starts at the top-left corner, and the arrow \(\vec{d}\) along the left side also starts at that same top-left corner and runs downwards. Coinitial vectors: \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{d}\).
_note: Read off Fig 10.6 on page 4 of the rendered chapter (arrowheads: a to the right, b downwards, c to the LEFT, d downwards).

solution: Equal vectors must have the same magnitude AND the same direction. In Fig 10.6 the side arrows \(\vec{b}\) (right side) and \(\vec{d}\) (left side) are both directed downwards and, the figure being a square, both have length equal to the side. Hence they have equal magnitude and identical direction. Equal vectors: \(\vec{b}\) and \(\vec{d}\).
_note: The other parallel pair, a and c, are NOT equal: the figure shows a directed to the right and c directed to the left, so c = -a.

solution: Vectors are collinear if they are parallel to the same line, whatever their magnitudes and directions. In Fig 10.6 the arrow \(\vec{a}\) along the top side points to the right while the arrow \(\vec{c}\) along the bottom side points to the left, so both are parallel to the same (horizontal) line and have the same length, but their directions are opposite, giving \(\vec{c} = -\vec{a}\). They are therefore collinear yet not equal. Collinear but not equal: \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{c}\).
_note: b and d are also collinear, but they are equal, so they do not answer this part.

solution: Since \(-\vec{a} = (-1)\vec{a}\), the vector \(-\vec{a}\) is a scalar multiple of \(\vec{a}\), so the two are parallel to the same line. Hence the statement is True.

Collinearity only requires the vectors to be parallel to the same line; it places no restriction on their lengths. For instance \(\hat{i}\) and \(2\hat{i}\) are collinear but have magnitudes 1 and 2. Hence the statement is False.

Equal magnitudes say nothing about direction. For instance \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\) both have magnitude 1, yet they are perpendicular and so are not parallel to the same line. Hence the statement is False.

Two collinear vectors of equal magnitude may still point in opposite directions. For instance \(\hat{i}\) and \(-\hat{i}\) are collinear and both have magnitude 1, but \(\hat{i} \ne -\hat{i}\). Hence the statement is False.

[Textbook misprint: the book prints the third basis vector of the first vector as a bare italic letter with no hat, while the other two on the same line and every other basis vector in the question carry one. Transcribed as printed; it is a typesetting slip and the answer is unaffected.] The magnitude of \(x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}\) is \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\). So \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{3}\); \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-7)^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 49 + 9} = \sqrt{62}\); \(|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3}} = 1\). Hence the magnitudes are \(\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{62}\) and \(1\).

Two vectors are different if their corresponding components differ, while their magnitudes may still agree. Take \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\). Then \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}\) and \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{9 + 4 + 1} = \sqrt{14}\). Hence \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\) are two different vectors having the same magnitude \(\sqrt{14}\).

Two vectors have the same direction when one is a positive scalar multiple of the other, their magnitudes being different. Take \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). Then \(\vec{b} = 2\vec{a}\), and both have the same unit vector \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\). Hence \(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) are two different vectors having the same direction.
Two vectors are equal only when their corresponding components are equal. Comparing \(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\) with \(x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}\) gives \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\).

For initial point \(P(2, 1)\) and terminal point \(Q(-5, 7)\), \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (-5 - 2)\hat{i} + (7 - 1)\hat{j} = -7\hat{i} + 6\hat{j}\). Hence the scalar components are \(-7\) and \(6\), and the vector components are \(-7\hat{i}\) and \(6\hat{j}\).

Add the corresponding components: \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = (1 - 2 + 1)\hat{i} + (-2 + 4 - 6)\hat{j} + (1 + 5 - 7)\hat{k}\). This gives \(0\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}\). Hence the sum is \(-4\hat{j} - \hat{k}\).

The unit vector along \(\vec{a}\) is \(\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}\). Here \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{6}\). Hence \(\hat{a} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\).

Here \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (4 - 1)\hat{i} + (5 - 2)\hat{j} + (6 - 3)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\), so \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}| = \sqrt{9 + 9 + 9} = 3\sqrt{3}\). Hence the required unit vector is \(\frac{3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\).

First, \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (2 - 1)\hat{i} + (-1 + 1)\hat{j} + (2 - 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} + \hat{k}\). Then \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = \sqrt{1 + 0 + 1} = \sqrt{2}\). Hence the required unit vector is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{i} + \hat{k})\).

Let \(\vec{v} = 5\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), so \(|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{25 + 1 + 4} = \sqrt{30}\). A vector of magnitude 8 along \(\vec{v}\) is \(8\,\frac{\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|}\). Hence the required vector is \(\frac{8}{\sqrt{30}}(5\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = \frac{40\hat{i} - 8\hat{j} + 16\hat{k}}{\sqrt{30}}\).

Two vectors are collinear when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Let \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = -4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\). Then \(-2\vec{a} = -4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 8\hat{k} = \vec{b}\), so \(\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}\) with \(\lambda = -2\). Hence \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are collinear.

The direction cosines of \(\vec{v} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}\) are \(\frac{x}{|\vec{v}|}, \frac{y}{|\vec{v}|}, \frac{z}{|\vec{v}|}\). Here \(|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}\). Hence the direction cosines are \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}, \frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}\).

Here \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (-1 - 1)\hat{i} + (-2 - 2)\hat{j} + (1 + 3)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\), so \(|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{4 + 16 + 16} = \sqrt{36} = 6\). Dividing the components by 6, the direction cosines are \(-\frac{1}{3}, -\frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\).

Let \(\vec{v} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), so \(|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{3}\). If \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are the angles \(\vec{v}\) makes with OX, OY, OZ, then \(\cos\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \(\cos\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \(\cos\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Since \(\cos\alpha = \cos\beta = \cos\gamma\), we get \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\). Hence \(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) is equally inclined to the axes OX, OY and OZ.

If R divides PQ internally in the ratio \(m : n\), then \(\vec{r} = \frac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}\). With \(\vec{p} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{q} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(m : n = 2 : 1\), \(\vec{r} = \frac{2(-\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) + (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})}{3} = \frac{-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}}{3}\). Hence the position vector of R is \(\frac{1}{3}(-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k})\).

If R divides PQ externally in the ratio \(m : n\), then \(\vec{r} = \frac{m\vec{q} - n\vec{p}}{m - n}\). With \(\vec{p} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{q} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(m : n = 2 : 1\), \(\vec{r} = \frac{2(-\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) - (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})}{2 - 1} = -3\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\). Hence the position vector of R is \(-3\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}\).

The position vector of the mid point of PQ is \(\frac{\vec{p} + \vec{q}}{2}\). Here \(\frac{(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}) + (4\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})}{2} = \frac{6\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}}{2}\). Hence the required position vector is \(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\).

Form the side vectors: \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\), \(\overrightarrow{BC} = \vec{c} - \vec{b} = -\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\), \(\overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{c} - \vec{a} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\). Then \(|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2 = 1 + 9 + 25 = 35\), \(|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2 = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6\) and \(|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2 = 1 + 4 + 36 = 41\). Since \(35 + 6 = 41\), we have \(|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{AC}|^2 = |\overrightarrow{BC}|^2\); equivalently \(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC} = 2 + 3 - 5 = 0\). Hence A, B, C form a right angled triangle, right angled at A.
Using \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta\), \(\cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{3}\times 2} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Hence \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\).

Let \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\). Then \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10\), while \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}\). So \(\cos\theta = \frac{10}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{14}} = \frac{5}{7}\). Hence \(\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)\).

The projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is \(\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\). Here \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (1)(1) + (-1)(1) = 0\) and \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{2}\). Hence the projection is \(\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\) (the two vectors are perpendicular).

The projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is \(\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\). Here \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (1)(7) + (3)(-1) + (7)(8) = 7 - 3 + 56 = 60\) and \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{49 + 1 + 64} = \sqrt{114}\). Hence the projection is \(\frac{60}{\sqrt{114}}\).

Write \(\vec{p} = \frac{1}{7}(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})\), \(\vec{q} = \frac{1}{7}(3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\), \(\vec{r} = \frac{1}{7}(6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k})\). Each bracket has magnitude \(\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} = \sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{49} = 7\), so \(|\vec{p}| = |\vec{q}| = |\vec{r}| = \frac{7}{7} = 1\) and each is a unit vector. For perpendicularity, \(49\,\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q} = 6 - 18 + 12 = 0\), \(49\,\vec{q}\cdot\vec{r} = 18 - 12 - 6 = 0\) and \(49\,\vec{r}\cdot\vec{p} = 12 + 6 - 18 = 0\). Hence all three dot products vanish, so the three unit vectors are mutually perpendicular.

Expanding, \((\vec{a} + \vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^2 - |\vec{b}|^2 = 8\). Putting \(|\vec{a}| = 8|\vec{b}|\) gives \(64|\vec{b}|^2 - |\vec{b}|^2 = 8\), so \(63|\vec{b}|^2 = 8\) and \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{\frac{8}{63}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{7}} = \frac{2\sqrt{14}}{21}\). Hence \(|\vec{b}| = \frac{2\sqrt{14}}{21}\) and \(|\vec{a}| = 8|\vec{b}| = \frac{16\sqrt{14}}{21}\).

Expand using distributivity of the scalar product: \((3\vec{a} - 5\vec{b})\cdot(2\vec{a} + 7\vec{b}) = 6\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} + 21\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} - 10\,\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a} - 35\,\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}\). Since \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}\), \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2\) and \(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{b}|^2\), this becomes \(6|\vec{a}|^2 + 11\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} - 35|\vec{b}|^2\).

Let \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = \lambda\), with \(\lambda > 0\). Then \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos 60^\circ = \lambda^2 \times \frac{1}{2}\). Equating to \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(\frac{\lambda^2}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\), so \(\lambda^2 = 1\) and, magnitudes being positive, \(\lambda = 1\). Hence \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 1\).

Expanding, \((\vec{x} - \vec{a})\cdot(\vec{x} + \vec{a}) = |\vec{x}|^2 - |\vec{a}|^2 = 12\). Since \(\vec{a}\) is a unit vector, \(|\vec{a}| = 1\), so \(|\vec{x}|^2 - 1 = 12\), giving \(|\vec{x}|^2 = 13\). Hence \(|\vec{x}| = \sqrt{13}\).

Here \(\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b} = (2 - \lambda)\hat{i} + (2 + 2\lambda)\hat{j} + (3 + \lambda)\hat{k}\). Perpendicularity to \(\vec{c}\) requires \((\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b})\cdot\vec{c} = 0\), that is \(3(2 - \lambda) + 1(2 + 2\lambda) + 0(3 + \lambda) = 0\). This gives \(6 - 3\lambda + 2 + 2\lambda = 0\), so \(8 - \lambda = 0\). Hence \(\lambda = 8\).

Take the scalar product of the two vectors: \((|\vec{a}|\vec{b} + |\vec{b}|\vec{a})\cdot(|\vec{a}|\vec{b} - |\vec{b}|\vec{a}) = |\vec{a}|^2(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}) - |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}) + |\vec{b}||\vec{a}|(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}) - |\vec{b}|^2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a})\). The two middle terms cancel because \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}\), leaving \(|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 - |\vec{b}|^2|\vec{a}|^2 = 0\). Since \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are non-zero, both vectors are non-zero, and a vanishing scalar product means they are perpendicular. Hence \(|\vec{a}|\vec{b} + |\vec{b}|\vec{a}\) is perpendicular to \(|\vec{a}|\vec{b} - |\vec{b}|\vec{a}\).

From \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2 = 0\) we get \(|\vec{a}| = 0\), so \(\vec{a} = \vec{0}\). But the zero vector has zero scalar product with every vector, so \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\) is automatically satisfied and carries no information about \(\vec{b}\). Hence nothing can be concluded about \(\vec{b}\): it may be any vector whatsoever.

Since \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}\), take the square of the magnitude: \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}|^2 = 0\). Expanding, \(|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{c}|^2 + 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 0\). The vectors being unit vectors, \(1 + 1 + 1 + 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 0\). Hence \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = -\frac{3}{2}\).

The converse would assert that \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\) forces \(\vec{a} = \vec{0}\) or \(\vec{b} = \vec{0}\). This fails, because the scalar product also vanishes when the two non-zero vectors are perpendicular. Take \(\vec{a} = \hat{i}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{j}\): then \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (1)(0) + (0)(1) + (0)(0) = 0\), yet \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 1\), so neither vector is the zero vector. Hence the converse need not be true.

Here \(\overrightarrow{BA} = (1 + 1)\hat{i} + (2 - 0)\hat{j} + (3 - 0)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC} = (0 + 1)\hat{i} + (1 - 0)\hat{j} + (2 - 0)\hat{k} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). Then \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC} = 2 + 2 + 6 = 10\), with \(|\overrightarrow{BA}| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{17}\) and \(|\overrightarrow{BC}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 4} = \sqrt{6}\). So \(\cos(\angle \mathrm{ABC}) = \frac{10}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt{6}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\). Hence \(\angle \mathrm{ABC} = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\right)\).

Form \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\), \(\overrightarrow{BC} = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC} = 2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\). Then \(|\overrightarrow{AB}| = |\overrightarrow{BC}| = \sqrt{1 + 16 + 16} = \sqrt{33}\) and \(|\overrightarrow{AC}| = \sqrt{4 + 64 + 64} = \sqrt{132} = 2\sqrt{33}\). Since \(|\overrightarrow{AB}| + |\overrightarrow{BC}| = \sqrt{33} + \sqrt{33} = 2\sqrt{33} = |\overrightarrow{AC}|\), the points A, B and C are collinear.

Let A, B, C have position vectors \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\), \(\vec{c} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\). Then \(\overrightarrow{CA} = \vec{a} - \vec{c} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{CB} = \vec{b} - \vec{c} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\), so \(\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB} = 2 + 3 - 5 = 0\). Equivalently \(|\overrightarrow{CA}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{CB}|^2 = 35 + 6 = 41 = |\overrightarrow{AB}|^2\). Hence the three points form a right angled triangle, right angled at C.

Compute the cross product by the determinant rule: \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}[(-7)(2) - (7)(-2)] - \hat{j}[(1)(2) - (7)(3)] + \hat{k}[(1)(-2) - (-7)(3)]\). This gives \(\hat{i}(-14 + 14) - \hat{j}(2 - 21) + \hat{k}(-2 + 21) = 19\hat{j} + 19\hat{k}\). Hence \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = \sqrt{0 + 361 + 361} = \sqrt{722} = 19\sqrt{2}\).

First \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{a} - \vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}\). A vector perpendicular to both is their cross product: \((\vec{a} + \vec{b})\times(\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = \hat{i}(4\cdot 4 - 0\cdot 0) - \hat{j}(4\cdot 4 - 0\cdot 2) + \hat{k}(4\cdot 0 - 4\cdot 2) = 16\hat{i} - 16\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{256 + 256 + 64} = \sqrt{576} = 24\). Hence the required unit vector is \(\pm\frac{1}{24}(16\hat{i} - 16\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}) = \pm\frac{1}{3}(2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})\).

For a unit vector the direction cosines satisfy \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\). Here \(\cos^2\frac{\pi}{3} + \cos^2\frac{\pi}{4} + \cos^2\theta = 1\), that is \(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} + \cos^2\theta = 1\), so \(\cos^2\theta = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(\cos\theta = \pm\frac{1}{2}\). Since \(\theta\) is acute, \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\), giving \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\). The components of \(\vec{a}\) are its direction cosines, so \(\vec{a} = \frac{1}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} + \frac{1}{2}\hat{k}\).

Expand using distributivity of the cross product: \((\vec{a} - \vec{b})\times(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = \vec{a}\times\vec{a} + \vec{a}\times\vec{b} - \vec{b}\times\vec{a} - \vec{b}\times\vec{b}\). Now \(\vec{a}\times\vec{a} = \vec{0}\), \(\vec{b}\times\vec{b} = \vec{0}\) and \(\vec{b}\times\vec{a} = -(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\). Hence the expression reduces to \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} + \vec{a}\times\vec{b} = 2(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\).

A vanishing cross product of two non-zero vectors means they are parallel, so their components are proportional: \(\frac{2}{1} = \frac{6}{\lambda} = \frac{27}{\mu}\). From \(\frac{6}{\lambda} = 2\) we get \(\lambda = 3\), and from \(\frac{27}{\mu} = 2\) we get \(\mu = \frac{27}{2}\). Hence \(\lambda = 3\) and \(\mu = \frac{27}{2}\).

Suppose both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) were non-zero, and let \(\theta\) be the angle between them. Then \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = 0\) forces \(\cos\theta = 0\), while \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta = 0\) forces \(\sin\theta = 0\). No angle satisfies \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\sin\theta = 0\) together, since \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\). Hence the supposition is impossible, and at least one of \(\vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\) must be the zero vector.

Here \(\vec{b} + \vec{c} = (b_1 + c_1)\hat{i} + (b_2 + c_2)\hat{j} + (b_3 + c_3)\hat{k}\). Expanding the determinant, \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = [a_2(b_3 + c_3) - a_3(b_2 + c_2)]\hat{i} + [a_3(b_1 + c_1) - a_1(b_3 + c_3)]\hat{j} + [a_1(b_2 + c_2) - a_2(b_1 + c_1)]\hat{k}\). Separating the \(b\)-terms from the \(c\)-terms in each component gives \([(a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\hat{i} + (a_3b_1 - a_1b_3)\hat{j} + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\hat{k}] + [(a_2c_3 - a_3c_2)\hat{i} + (a_3c_1 - a_1c_3)\hat{j} + (a_1c_2 - a_2c_1)\hat{k}]\). Hence \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a}\times\vec{b} + \vec{a}\times\vec{c}\).

The converse would assert that \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \vec{0}\) forces \(\vec{a} = \vec{0}\) or \(\vec{b} = \vec{0}\). This is not true, because the cross product also vanishes when the two non-zero vectors are parallel, \(\sin\theta\) being 0. Take \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), so that \(\vec{b} = 2\vec{a}\). Then \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}(2 - 2) - \hat{j}(2 - 2) + \hat{k}(2 - 2) = \vec{0}\), yet neither vector is the zero vector. Hence the converse is not true.

The area of a triangle on adjacent sides \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) is \(\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|\). Here \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC} = 0\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\), so \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC} = \hat{i}(2\cdot 3 - 3\cdot 4) - \hat{j}(1\cdot 3 - 3\cdot 0) + \hat{k}(1\cdot 4 - 2\cdot 0) = -6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{36 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{61}\). Hence the area is \(\frac{\sqrt{61}}{2}\) square units.

The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) is \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|\). Here \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}[(-1)(1) - (3)(-7)] - \hat{j}[(1)(1) - (3)(2)] + \hat{k}[(1)(-7) - (-1)(2)] = \hat{i}(-1 + 21) - \hat{j}(1 - 6) + \hat{k}(-7 + 2) = 20\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\). So \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = \sqrt{400 + 25 + 25} = \sqrt{450} = 15\sqrt{2}\). Hence the area is \(15\sqrt{2}\) square units.

A unit vector in the XY-plane making an angle \(\theta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis is \(\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + \sin\theta\,\hat{j}\). Putting \(\theta = 30^\circ\) gives \(\cos 30^\circ\,\hat{i} + \sin 30^\circ\,\hat{j}\). Hence the required unit vector is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{1}{2}\hat{j}\).

The vector joining P to Q is \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j} + (z_2 - z_1)\hat{k}\). Hence its scalar components are \(x_2 - x_1\), \(y_2 - y_1\) and \(z_2 - z_1\), and its magnitude is \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}| = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}\).

Take \(\hat{i}\) towards east and \(\hat{j}\) towards north. The first walk of 4 km towards west is \(-4\hat{i}\). The second walk is 3 km in the direction \(30^\circ\) east of north, whose unit vector is \(\sin 30^\circ\,\hat{i} + \cos 30^\circ\,\hat{j}\), giving \(3\left(\frac{1}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}\right) = \frac{3}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}\). Adding, the total displacement is \(\left(-4 + \frac{3}{2}\right)\hat{i} + \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j} = -\frac{5}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}\), of magnitude \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{4} + \frac{27}{4}} = \sqrt{13}\). Hence the girl's displacement from her initial point is \(-\frac{5}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{j}\), that is \(\sqrt{13}\) km.

No, it is not true in general. By the triangle inequality \(|\vec{b} + \vec{c}| \le |\vec{b}| + |\vec{c}|\), with equality only when \(\vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\) point in the same direction (or one of them is the zero vector). For a counter-example take \(\vec{b} = \hat{i}\) and \(\vec{c} = \hat{j}\), so \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}\). Then \(|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2}\) whereas \(|\vec{b}| + |\vec{c}| = 1 + 1 = 2\), and \(\sqrt{2} \ne 2\). Hence \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| + |\vec{c}|\) need not hold.

The vector \(x(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\) has magnitude \(|x|\sqrt{1 + 1 + 1} = |x|\sqrt{3}\). For it to be a unit vector, \(|x|\sqrt{3} = 1\), so \(|x| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Hence \(x = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

The resultant is \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (2 + 1)\hat{i} + (3 - 2)\hat{j} + (-1 + 1)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j}\), with \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = \sqrt{9 + 1} = \sqrt{10}\). A vector of magnitude 5 parallel to it is \(\pm 5\,\frac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|}\). Hence the required vector is \(\pm\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}}(3\hat{i} + \hat{j}) = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(15\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})\).

Compute \(2\vec{a} - \vec{b} + 3\vec{c} = (2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) - (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) + (3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})\). Collecting components, this is \((2 - 2 + 3)\hat{i} + (2 + 1 - 6)\hat{j} + (2 - 3 + 3)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{9 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{22}\). Hence a unit vector parallel to it is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{22}}(3\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\).

Form \(\overrightarrow{AB} = 4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC} = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}\). Since \(\overrightarrow{BC} = \frac{3}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}\), the two are parallel and share the point B, so A, B and C are collinear. Their magnitudes are \(|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{16 + 4 + 36} = \sqrt{56} = 2\sqrt{14}\) and \(|\overrightarrow{BC}| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 81} = \sqrt{126} = 3\sqrt{14}\), so \(\mathrm{AB} : \mathrm{BC} = 2 : 3\). Checking by the section formula, \(\frac{3\vec{a} + 2\vec{c}}{5} = \frac{3(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}) + 2(11\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 7\hat{k})}{5} = 5\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\), which is the position vector of B. Hence B divides AC internally in the ratio \(2 : 3\).

For external division in the ratio \(m : n\), \(\vec{r} = \frac{m\vec{q} - n\vec{p}}{m - n}\). With \(\vec{p} = 2\vec{a} + \vec{b}\), \(\vec{q} = \vec{a} - 3\vec{b}\) and \(m : n = 1 : 2\), \(\vec{r} = \frac{(\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}) - 2(2\vec{a} + \vec{b})}{1 - 2} = \frac{-3\vec{a} - 5\vec{b}}{-1} = 3\vec{a} + 5\vec{b}\). To show P is the mid point of RQ, take \(\frac{\vec{r} + \vec{q}}{2} = \frac{(3\vec{a} + 5\vec{b}) + (\vec{a} - 3\vec{b})}{2} = \frac{4\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}}{2} = 2\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{p}\). Hence the position vector of R is \(3\vec{a} + 5\vec{b}\), and P is the mid point of RQ.

Let \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\) be the adjacent sides. One diagonal is \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\), of magnitude \(\sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} = 7\), so the unit vector along it is \(\frac{1}{7}(3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\). (The other diagonal is \(\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\), giving the unit vector \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{69}}(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 8\hat{k})\).) For the area, \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}[(-4)(-3) - (5)(-2)] - \hat{j}[(2)(-3) - (5)(1)] + \hat{k}[(2)(-2) - (-4)(1)] = 22\hat{i} + 11\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}\), so \(|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = \sqrt{484 + 121} = \sqrt{605} = 11\sqrt{5}\). Hence the unit vector along the diagonal is \(\frac{1}{7}(3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\) and the area is \(11\sqrt{5}\) square units.

Let the vector make angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) with OX, OY, OZ, so its direction cosines are \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\) and \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\). Being equally inclined to the axes means \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma\), so \(\cos\alpha = \cos\beta = \cos\gamma = t\), say. Substituting, \(3t^2 = 1\), so \(t = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Hence the direction cosines are \(\pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the third component with a PLUS sign. That vector satisfies none of the three conditions the question states — it is perpendicular to neither of the first two vectors, and its dot product with the third is not 15. Changing that one sign to a MINUS makes all three conditions hold exactly, and every component magnitude in the printed key is otherwise correct, so a single dropped sign is the whole error. The answer below is the corrected vector.] Since \(\vec{d}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\), it is parallel to \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\), so write \(\vec{d} = \lambda(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\). Here \(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}[(4)(7) - (2)(-2)] - \hat{j}[(1)(7) - (2)(3)] + \hat{k}[(1)(-2) - (4)(3)] = 32\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 14\hat{k}\). Then \(\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}) = (2)(32) + (-1)(-1) + (4)(-14) = 64 + 1 - 56 = 9\), so the condition \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = 15\) gives \(9\lambda = 15\), that is \(\lambda = \frac{5}{3}\). Hence \(\vec{d} = \frac{5}{3}(32\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 14\hat{k}) = \frac{1}{3}(160\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 70\hat{k})\).

The sum of the two vectors is \(\vec{s} = (2 + \lambda)\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\), with \(|\vec{s}| = \sqrt{(2 + \lambda)^2 + 40}\). The stated condition is \((\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\cdot\frac{\vec{s}}{|\vec{s}|} = 1\), that is \(\frac{(2 + \lambda) + 6 - 2}{\sqrt{(2 + \lambda)^2 + 40}} = 1\), so \(\lambda + 6 = \sqrt{(\lambda + 2)^2 + 40}\) with \(\lambda + 6 \ge 0\). Squaring, \(\lambda^2 + 12\lambda + 36 = \lambda^2 + 4\lambda + 44\), giving \(8\lambda = 8\). Hence \(\lambda = 1\) (checking: \(\vec{s} = 3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\), \(|\vec{s}| = 7\), and \(\frac{3 + 6 - 2}{7} = 1\)).

[Textbook misprint: the question prints "show that the vector \(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = 15\) is equally inclined to \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\)". That clause is a scalar equation, not a vector, and \(\vec{d}\) is nowhere defined in this question; it is the closing condition of the preceding question on the same page, carried over in error. The intended vector is \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}\), and it is solved as such below.] Let \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = |\vec{c}| = \lambda\), with \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} = \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = 0\) since the vectors are mutually perpendicular. Put \(\vec{s} = \vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}\). Then \(|\vec{s}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{c}|^2 + 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 3\lambda^2\), so \(|\vec{s}| = \sqrt{3}\,\lambda\). Also \(\vec{s}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2 + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = \lambda^2\), and likewise \(\vec{s}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{s}\cdot\vec{c} = \lambda^2\). Hence if \(\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3\) are the angles \(\vec{s}\) makes with \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}\), \(\cos\theta_1 = \frac{\lambda^2}{(\sqrt{3}\lambda)(\lambda)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \cos\theta_2 = \cos\theta_3\). Therefore \(\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\), so \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}\) is equally inclined to \(\vec{a}, \vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c}\).

Solved for the intended reading a + b + c, with the [Textbook misprint: ...] bracket opening the solution.

solution: Expanding the left side, \((\vec{a} + \vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} + 2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}\). Hence \((\vec{a} + \vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2\) holds if and only if \(2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\), that is if and only if \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0\). Since \(\vec{a} \ne \vec{0}\) and \(\vec{b} \ne \vec{0}\), the condition \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = 0\) is equivalent to \(\cos\theta = 0\), i.e. to \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) being perpendicular. This proves the statement in both directions.
